title: Refraction of Light: Causes, Change of Speed & Optical Density
tagline: Bending of light across optical media, rarer vs denser media, and speed variations.
theoryHtml:
1. What is Refraction of Light?

When a beam of light travelling through one transparent medium enters obliquely into another transparent medium of differing optical density, it deviates from its original straight path at the interface between the two media. This phenomenon is called the refraction of light.

2. The Fundamental Cause of Refraction

Light refracts because its speed changes as it crosses from one medium into another. While light travels at $c \approx 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$ in vacuum (and air), it slows down to approximately $2.25 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$ in water and $2.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$ in crown glass. The wavefronts change speed at different times across the oblique boundary, bending the ray.

3. Optically Rarer vs Optically Denser Media

  • Rarer to Denser (e.g., Air to Glass): The speed of light decreases. The ray bends towards the normal ($\angle i > \angle r$).
  • Denser to Rarer (e.g., Glass to Air): The speed of light increases. The ray bends away from the normal ($\angle i < \angle r$).

4. Optical Density vs Mass Density

Optical density is the ability of a medium to refract light and is inversely proportional to the speed of light in that medium. It must not be confused with mass density (mass per unit volume). For instance, kerosene has a lower mass density than water (kerosene floats on water), yet kerosene is optically denser than water because the speed of light is lower in kerosene than in water.
pointsToRemember: Refraction is the bending of light when passing obliquely between media of differing optical densities.
The fundamental cause of refraction is the difference in the speed of light in different media.
Ray bending rule: Rarer $\rightarrow$ Denser bends TOWARDS the normal; Denser $\rightarrow$ Rarer bends AWAY from the normal.
keyNotes: Optical density is not the same as mass density: kerosene floats on water (lower mass density) but refracts light more strongly (higher optical density).

questions.question: The bending of a ray of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another of different optical density is called:
questions.explanation: Refraction is the change in direction of light propagation caused by a change in wave propagation speed across different media interfaces.

questions.question: What is the fundamental physical cause behind the phenomenon of refraction of light?
options: Change in the frequency of light
Change in the speed of light as it enters from one medium into another
questions.answer: Change in the speed of light as it enters from one medium into another
questions.explanation: Light travels at different velocities in different media; this difference in phase speed causes wave front refraction at oblique boundaries.

questions.question: Why does light bend when entering obliquely from air into water?
options: One side of the incident light wave front enters the optically denser water first and slows down before the other side, pivoting the wave direction towards the normal
questions.answer: One side of the incident light wave front enters the optically denser water first and slows down before the other side, pivoting the wave direction towards the normal
questions.explanation: Huygens' wave principle: oblique incidence causes leading wave front edges to decelerate first, steering the propagation vector towards the normal.

questions.question: When a ray of light enters obliquely from air into water, how does it bend relative to the normal?
options: It bends away from the normal
It bends towards the normal because water is optically denser than air
It does not bend at all
It reflects straight back into air
questions.answer: It bends towards the normal because water is optically denser than air
questions.explanation: Light travels slower in water than in air; passing from an optically rarer to a denser medium causes the ray to bend towards the normal (∠r < ∠i).

questions.question: What happens to a ray of light that strikes the interface of two transparent media at normal incidence (perpendicular to the surface)?
options: It passes straight through into the second medium without any deviation
questions.answer: It passes straight through into the second medium without any deviation
questions.explanation: At normal incidence (∠i = 0°), all parts of the incident wavefront slow down simultaneously, so light travels straight without bending (∠r = 0°).

questions.question: Which of the following optical media has the highest optical density (lowest speed of light)?
questions.explanation: Diamond has an exceptionally high refractive index (n ≈ 2.42), meaning light slows down to ~1.24 × 10^8 m/s, giving it the highest optical density.

questions.question: Kerosene floats on top of water, yet it is described as optically denser than water. What does this prove?
options: Optical density is completely independent of mass density
Light travels faster in kerosene than in water
questions.answer: Optical density is completely independent of mass density
questions.explanation: Mass density is mass/volume, whereas optical density measures light speed retardation; kerosene has lower mass density but slows light more than water.

questions.question: When light passes from glass into air, what happens to its speed and direction of travel?
options: Speed decreases and ray bends towards normal
Speed increases and ray bends away from the normal
Speed remains constant and ray stops
Speed increases but ray bends towards normal
questions.answer: Speed increases and ray bends away from the normal
questions.explanation: Moving from denser (glass) to rarer (air), light speeds up, causing the ray to bend away from the normal (∠r > ∠i).

questions.question: Which physical characteristic of a light wave remains completely UNCHANGED when it undergoes refraction?
questions.explanation: Frequency is determined solely by the vibrating light source and remains strictly invariant as light traverses different media (v = fλ).

questions.question: Why does a straight pencil partially immersed in water appear bent and broken at the water-air interface?
options: Water chemically dissolves the wooden pencil
Light rays originating from the immersed portion refract away from the normal as they emerge into air
The pencil physically bends due to water pressure
Total internal reflection inside the wood
questions.answer: Light rays originating from the immersed portion refract away from the normal as they emerge into air
questions.explanation: Light rays emerging from water into air bend away from the normal, making the submerged portion appear displaced upwards to an observer.

title: Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab & Lateral Displacement
tagline: Two refracting surfaces, angle of emergence e = angle of incidence i, and lateral shift.
theoryHtml:
1. Double Refraction in a Rectangular Glass Slab

When a ray of light passes through a parallel-sided rectangular glass slab, it undergoes refraction at two parallel interfaces:

  1. First Surface (Air $\rightarrow$ Glass): Ray enters from an optically rarer medium (air) to an optically denser medium (glass). It bends towards the normal ($\angle i > \angle r_1$).
  2. Second Surface (Glass $\rightarrow$ Air): The refracted ray travels through glass and reaches the opposite parallel face. Here, it exits from denser glass into rarer air, bending away from the normal by an equal amount ($\angle r_2 < \angle e$).

2. Parallelism of Incident and Emergent Rays ($\angle i = \angle e$)

Because the two refracting surfaces are parallel, the extent of bending towards the normal at the first surface is exactly equal and opposite to the extent of bending away from the normal at the second surface. Consequently:

$$\text{Angle of Incidence } (\angle i) = \text{Angle of Emergence } (\angle e)$$

The emergent ray is strictly parallel to the original path of the incident ray.

3. Lateral Displacement ($d$)

Although the emergent ray does not change its direction, it is physically shifted sideways relative to the incident ray path. This perpendicular separation between the original incident path and the emergent ray is called lateral displacement (or lateral shift). Lateral displacement increases with:

  • Increasing thickness ($t$) of the glass slab.
  • Increasing angle of incidence ($\angle i$).
  • Increasing refractive index ($n$) of the glass.
pointsToRemember: In a parallel rectangular glass slab, the emergent ray is always parallel to the incident ray ($\angle i = \angle e$).
Lateral displacement is the perpendicular sideways distance between the incident and emergent ray paths.
Lateral displacement increases with slab thickness, higher angle of incidence, and higher refractive index.
keyNotes: The emergent ray does not suffer any net angular deviation (angular deviation $\delta = 0^\circ$); it suffers only a parallel lateral displacement.

questions.question: In the refraction of light through a rectangular glass slab with parallel faces, why is the emergent ray PARALLEL to the incident ray?
options: The extent of bending (refraction angle) at the first air-glass interface is exactly equal and opposite to the bending at the second glass-air interface
Light rays cannot bend in glass
The slab acts like a mirror
questions.answer: The extent of bending (refraction angle) at the first air-glass interface is exactly equal and opposite to the bending at the second glass-air interface
questions.explanation: Because opposite faces AB and CD are parallel, the angle of refraction at the first face equals the angle of incidence at the second face, causing the emergent ray to exit parallel to the incident path with a slight lateral displacement.

questions.question: When two thin lenses of powers P₁ = +2.0 D and P₂ = +0.25 D are placed in contact, what is the net power (P) of the combination?
questions.explanation: Net power of thin lenses in contact is the algebraic sum: P = P₁ + P₂ = +2.0 D + 0.25 D = +2.25 D.

questions.question: Which of the following materials CANNOT be used to make an optical lens?
questions.explanation: Clay is an opaque material that does not transmit or refract light, and thus cannot be fabricated into a lens.

questions.question: A spherical mirror and a thin spherical lens each have a focal length of -15 cm. What are the mirror and lens likely to be?
questions.explanation: Under Cartesian sign conventions, a negative focal length (f = -15 cm) corresponds to both a concave mirror and a concave lens.

questions.question: What is the mathematical relationship between the angle of incidence (i) and the angle of emergence (e) for a parallel-faced glass slab?
questions.explanation: Because the two refracting faces are strictly parallel, the second refraction undoes the angular deviation of the first, so ∠i = ∠e.

questions.question: What is the perpendicular distance between the original incident ray direction and the emergent ray after passing through a glass slab called?
questions.explanation: Lateral displacement is the perpendicular sideways shift between the incident ray path and the parallel emergent ray.

questions.question: How does the magnitude of lateral displacement change if the thickness of the glass slab is doubled?
questions.explanation: Lateral displacement is directly proportional to the thickness of the refracting slab (d ∝ t).

questions.question: What is the net angular deviation produced by a parallel-sided rectangular glass slab on an incident ray of light?
questions.explanation: Since the emergent ray emerges parallel to the incident ray, the angular deviation is zero (δ = 0°).

questions.question: If a printed page is viewed through a thick glass slab, why do the letters appear raised closer to the surface?
options: Refraction of light emerging from the glass into air makes the apparent depth less than the real depth
Atmospheric pressure pushes the ink upwards
questions.answer: Refraction of light emerging from the glass into air makes the apparent depth less than the real depth
questions.explanation: Apparent depth = Real depth / n. Because n > 1 for glass, apparent depth is smaller, making letters appear raised.

questions.question: In an experiment tracing light through a rectangular glass slab, if ∠i = 45°, what is the expected angle of emergence ∠e?
questions.explanation: Since ∠i = ∠e in a parallel slab, when ∠i = 45°, ∠e must also equal 45°.

title: The Laws of Refraction & Snell's Law of Refraction
tagline: Coplanar rays, the constant ratio sin i / sin r, and physical meaning of the constant.
theoryHtml:
1. The First Law of Refraction

The incident ray, the refracted ray, and the normal to the interface of two transparent media at the point of incidence, all lie in the same geometric plane.

2. The Second Law of Refraction (Snell's Law)

Formulated in 1621 by Dutch astronomer Willebrord Snell, the second law states:

"The ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant for a given pair of media and for light of a given wavelength (colour)."

Mathematically expressed as:

$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \text{constant} = n_{21}$$

Where:

  • $i$ is the angle of incidence in Medium 1.
  • $r$ is the angle of refraction in Medium 2.
  • $n_{21}$ is the relative refractive index of Medium 2 with respect to Medium 1.

3. Conditions for Snell's Law

Snell's law applies for all oblique angles of incidence ($0^\circ < i < 90^\circ$). For normal incidence ($i = 0^\circ$), $\sin 0^\circ = 0$, which implies $\sin r = 0 \implies r = 0^\circ$, meaning the ray passes undeviated.
pointsToRemember: First Law: Incident ray, refracted ray, and normal at point of incidence all lie in the same plane.
Snell's Law: $\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \text{constant} = n_{21}$ for a given pair of media.
The constant represents the relative refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.
keyNotes: Snell's law holds constant only for monochromatic light (light of a single specific colour/wavelength), as refractive index varies slightly with wavelength (dispersion).

questions.question: No matter how far you stand from a mirror, your image always appears erect. The mirror is likely to be:
questions.explanation: Both plane mirrors (m = +1) and convex mirrors (0 < m < 1) always produce upright, virtual images regardless of object distance.

questions.question: Which lens would you prefer to use as a magnifying glass while reading very small letters in a dictionary?
options: A concave lens of focal length 5 cm
A convex lens of short focal length 5 cm
A convex lens of focal length 50 cm
A concave lens of focal length 50 cm
questions.answer: A convex lens of short focal length 5 cm
questions.explanation: A convex lens of shorter focal length (f = 5 cm) has higher optical power (P = 100/5 = +20 D) and produces greater angular magnification (M = 1 + D/f).

questions.question: Why does a pencil partly immersed in water in a glass tumbler appear bent and displaced at the air-water interface?
options: Water chemically dissolves the pencil wood
Light rays coming from the immersed portion of the pencil refract and bend away from the normal upon exiting water into air
Water reflects all rays into the ceiling
questions.answer: Light rays coming from the immersed portion of the pencil refract and bend away from the normal upon exiting water into air
questions.explanation: Rays from the submerged pencil bend away from the normal at the water-air interface, making the submerged part appear shifted upwards.

questions.question: What is the mathematical formulation of Snell's Law of Refraction?
questions.explanation: Snell's Law states that the ratio of sin i to sin r is a constant for a given pair of optical media.

questions.question: What physical quantity is represented by the constant in the equation sin i / sin r = constant?
options: The speed of sound in air
The relative refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first medium
The focal length of the surface
The mass density of the boundary
questions.answer: The relative refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first medium
questions.explanation: The constant represents n21, the refractive index of Medium 2 relative to Medium 1.

questions.question: If a ray of light enters from air into glass such that the angle of incidence is 60° and the angle of refraction is 30°, what is the refractive index of glass with respect to air?
Does Snell's Law apply when a ray of light strikes an optical interface normally (angle of incidence i = 0°)?
options: Yes, with sin 0° = 0, sin r = 0, which correctly yields r = 0° (undeviated ray)
Only if both media are liquids
questions.answer: Yes, with sin 0° = 0, sin r = 0, which correctly yields r = 0° (undeviated ray)
questions.explanation: At i = 0°, sin i = 0, requiring sin r = 0, which gives r = 0°, meaning the ray travels straight without deviation.

questions.question: Why does Snell's Law specify 'for light of a given wavelength'?
options: Because light changes frequency in glass
Because different wavelengths (colours) of light travel at slightly different speeds in a material medium, giving different refractive indices
Because only green light obeys physics
questions.answer: Because different wavelengths (colours) of light travel at slightly different speeds in a material medium, giving different refractive indices
questions.explanation: Refractive index varies with wavelength (Cauchy's dispersion relation), causing violet light to bend more than red light.

questions.question: If the refractive index of a medium with respect to air is 2, what is the angle of refraction when the angle of incidence is 30°?
Who independently formulated the sine law of refraction in 1621?
questions.explanation: Dutch astronomer and mathematician Willebrord Snell discovered the law in 1621, hence named Snell's Law.

title: Refractive Index: Absolute ($n = c/v$) & Relative Index ($n_{21} = v_1/v_2$)
tagline: Speed of light in media, unitless ratio, and optical density relationships.
theoryHtml:
1. Absolute Refractive Index ($n$)

When light travels from vacuum (or air) into a given material medium, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum ($c$) to the speed of light in that medium ($v$) is defined as the absolute refractive index ($n$) of the medium:

$$n = \frac{c}{v} = \frac{\text{Speed of light in vacuum}}{\text{Speed of light in medium}}$$

Because it is a pure ratio of two identical physical quantities (speeds), the refractive index has no units and no dimensions. Since the speed of light in any material medium is always strictly less than $c$, $n \ge 1.0$ for all physical media:

  • Air: $n \approx 1.0003$
  • Water: $n = 1.33 = \frac{4}{3}$
  • Crown Glass: $n = 1.52 \approx \frac{3}{2}$
  • Diamond: $n = 2.42$

2. Relative Refractive Index ($n_{21}$)

When light travels from Medium 1 into Medium 2, the relative refractive index of Medium 2 with respect to Medium 1 ($n_{21}$) is given by:

$$n_{21} = \frac{v_1}{v_2} = \frac{c/v_2}{c/v_1} = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$$

Conversely, the refractive index of Medium 1 with respect to Medium 2 is the reciprocal:

$$n_{12} = \frac{1}{n_{21}}$$
pointsToRemember: Absolute refractive index: $n = c/v$; it is unitless and always $\ge 1$.
Relative refractive index: $n_{21} = v_1 / v_2 = n_2 / n_1$.
Reciprocity relation: $n_{12} = 1 / n_{21}$.
keyNotes: Higher refractive index means light travels slower in that medium; diamond ($n = 2.42$) slows light down to just $1.24 	imes 10^8\text{ m/s}$.

questions.question: When a thick rectangular glass slab is placed over printed text, why do the letters appear raised when viewed from above?
options: Due to refraction of light bending away from the normal as it emerges from denser glass into rarer air, creating an apparent virtual depth
questions.answer: Due to refraction of light bending away from the normal as it emerges from denser glass into rarer air, creating an apparent virtual depth
questions.explanation: Refraction creates an apparent depth (d' = d / n), raising the apparent position of the text towards the observer.

questions.question: When an object placed in front of a spherical mirror is moved from 40 cm to 20 cm from the pole, the magnification remains POSITIVE but INCREASES from +0.2 to +0.5. What type of mirror is it?
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors always produce positive magnification less than 1 (0 < m < 1). As the object approaches the pole (from 40 cm to 20 cm), the diminished image grows larger towards m = 1.

questions.question: In which of the following optical media will the critical angle for total internal reflection with air be the SMALLEST?
questions.explanation: Critical angle sin C = 1 / n. Diamond has the largest n (2.42), giving the smallest critical angle (C ≈ 24.4°), which traps light inside for brilliant sparkling.

questions.question: What is the formula for the absolute refractive index (n) of a medium?
questions.explanation: Absolute refractive index is the ratio of speed of light in vacuum (c) to speed in the medium (v): n = c/v.

questions.question: What is the speed of light in crown glass having an absolute refractive index of n = 1.50? (Given c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
What are the SI units of refractive index?
questions.explanation: Being a ratio of two velocities (m/s divided by m/s), refractive index is a pure dimensionless number.

questions.question: If the refractive index of water is 4/3 and glass is 3/2, what is the refractive index of glass with respect to water?
If the refractive index of glass with respect to air is 1.5, what is the refractive index of air with respect to glass?
questions.explanation: By the reciprocity principle, n_ag = 1 / n_ga = 1 / 1.5 = 2/3 ≈ 0.67.

questions.question: Diamond has a refractive index of 2.42. What is the speed of light inside diamond? (c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
Can the absolute refractive index of any physical medium ever be less than 1.0?
options: No, because nothing can travel faster than the speed of light in vacuum (c)
questions.answer: No, because nothing can travel faster than the speed of light in vacuum (c)
questions.explanation: Since c is the universal maximum speed of light, v <= c, meaning n = c/v is always >= 1.0.

title: Spherical Lenses: Convex vs Concave Anatomy & Optical Centre
tagline: Converging vs diverging lenses, optical centre O, principal foci F1 and F2.
theoryHtml:
1. What is a Spherical Lens?

A spherical lens is a piece of transparent optical material (such as glass or plastic) bounded by two spherical surfaces, or by one spherical surface and one plane surface:

  • Convex Lens (Double Convex / Converging Lens): Thicker at the middle and thinner at the edges. When a parallel beam of light strikes a convex lens, it refracts and converges to a real focus on the opposite side.
  • Concave Lens (Double Concave / Diverging Lens): Thicker at the edges and thinner at the middle. It refracts parallel rays outward, causing them to diverge as if originating from a virtual focus on the incident side.

2. Essential Lens Terminology

  • Optical Centre ($O$): The central point of the lens on its principal axis. A ray of light passing through the optical centre suffers zero net deviation and passes straight through.
  • Centres of Curvature ($C_1, C_2$ or $2F_1, 2F_2$): The centres of the two spheres forming the two curved surfaces.
  • Principal Axis: The imaginary line connecting both centres of curvature and passing through $O$.
  • Principal Foci ($F_1, F_2$): A lens has two principal foci on either side of the optical centre. For a thin lens, both focal lengths are equal ($OF_1 = OF_2 = f$).
pointsToRemember: A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges light; a concave lens is thinner in the middle and diverges light.
A ray passing through the optical centre ($O$) passes straight through without deviation.
A lens has two symmetrical principal foci ($F_1$ and $F_2$) equidistant from $O$ ($f = OF$).
keyNotes: A convex lens behaves as a converging lens when placed in a medium with a lower refractive index (like air), but would diverge light if submerged in a medium with a higher refractive index than the lens material!

questions.question: A lens which is thinner in the middle and thicker at the edges, and diverges a parallel beam of light rays, is called a:
questions.explanation: A double concave lens is thinner at the centre and diverges incident parallel rays so they appear to emanate from a virtual focus.

questions.question: The central point of a spherical lens through which a ray of light passes without suffering any angular deviation is called its:
questions.explanation: The optical centre (O) is the central nodal point of a lens; rays passing through O proceed undeviated.

questions.question: An object is placed at a distance equal to focal length (u = -f) in front of a convex lens. Where is the image formed, and what is its nature?
options: At infinity; Highly enlarged, real and inverted
Between O and F₂; Virtual and erect
questions.answer: At infinity; Highly enlarged, real and inverted
questions.explanation: 1/v = 1/f + 1/(-f) = 0 ⇒ v = ∞. Refracted rays emerge parallel and meet at infinity, forming an infinitely magnified real inverted image.

questions.question: What is the central point of a spherical lens through which a ray of light passes without suffering any deviation called?
questions.explanation: A ray passing through the optical centre (O) traverses the lens undeviated along a straight line.

questions.question: Which type of lens is thicker in the middle and thinner at the perimeter edges?
questions.explanation: A double convex lens bulges outwards at the centre and tapers towards the outer edges.

questions.question: Why is a double convex lens referred to as a 'converging lens'?
options: It scatters light in all directions
It bends parallel incident light rays inward to intersect at a common real focal point
questions.answer: It bends parallel incident light rays inward to intersect at a common real focal point
questions.explanation: Parallel rays entering a convex lens refract inward towards the principal axis, converging at the focal point.

questions.question: Why is a double concave lens referred to as a 'diverging lens'?
options: It focuses parallel rays into a bright spot
It refracts parallel incident rays outward, causing them to spread apart as if radiating from a virtual focus
questions.answer: It refracts parallel incident rays outward, causing them to spread apart as if radiating from a virtual focus
questions.explanation: A concave lens bends rays away from the principal axis, causing them to diverge outward.

questions.question: How many principal foci does a standard thin spherical lens possess?
options: Two (one on each side: F1 and F2)
questions.answer: Two (one on each side: F1 and F2)
questions.explanation: Because light can enter from either the left or right face, a lens possesses two principal foci (F1 and F2).

questions.question: What is the linear distance from the optical centre (O) to either principal focus of a thin lens called?
questions.explanation: The distance OF from the optical centre to the principal focus is the focal length f.

questions.question: A student burns a small hole in a dry leaf using a lens under bright sunlight. What type of lens did the student use?
questions.explanation: A convex lens converges the parallel rays of the sun onto a tiny real focal spot, concentrating heat to ignite the leaf.

title: Image Formation by Convex Lens: The Six Object Positions
tagline: Real vs virtual images, magnification changes, and the magnifying glass condition.
theoryHtml:
1. Image Formation Summary for Convex Lens

A convex lens forms real, inverted images for most object positions, but forms an erect, virtual image when the object is placed close to the lens:

Object PositionImage PositionImage SizeNature
At InfinityAt Focus ($F_2$)Highly diminished (point-sized)Real and inverted
Beyond $2F_1$Between $F_2$ and $2F_2$DiminishedReal and inverted
At $2F_1$At $2F_2$Same size as object ($m = -1$)Real and inverted
Between $F_1$ and $2F_1$Beyond $2F_2$Enlarged (magnified)Real and inverted
At Focus ($F_1$)At InfinityInfinitely large (highly enlarged)Real and inverted
Between $O$ and $F_1$On same side as objectEnlarged (magnified)Virtual and erect

2. The Simple Magnifying Glass

When an object (such as small text or a watch gear) is placed within the focal length of a convex lens (between $O$ and $F_1$), the refracted rays diverge on the opposite side. When projected backwards, they form an erect, highly magnified, virtual image on the same side. This is the operating principle of a simple microscope (magnifying glass).
pointsToRemember: Object at $2F_1$ forms an image at $2F_2$, real, inverted, and of the exact same size ($m = -1$).
Object at $F_1$ forms an image at infinity (parallel refracted rays).
Object between $O$ and $F_1$ produces a virtual, erect, and magnified image on the same side (magnifying glass).
keyNotes: Covering one half of a convex lens with black paper does NOT produce half an image; it forms the complete full image, but with reduced brightness (intensity) because fewer rays contribute.

questions.question: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens to obtain a real image of the EXACT SAME size as the object on a screen?
options: Between optical centre O and focus F₁
questions.explanation: Placing an object at 2F₁ of a convex lens forms an inverted, real image of identical size at 2F₂ on the other side (m = -1).

questions.question: Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens so that it functions as a simple magnifying glass (producing a virtual, erect, and magnified image)?
options: Between the principal focus (F₁) and the optical centre (O)
questions.answer: Between the principal focus (F₁) and the optical centre (O)
questions.explanation: When an object is placed within the focal length (between F₁ and O), a convex lens forms an enlarged, upright, virtual image on the same side as the object.

questions.question: If one-half of a convex lens is covered with black opaque paper, will the lens still form a complete image of an object?
options: No, only half of the image will be formed
Yes, a complete image of the entire object will still be formed, but its brightness (intensity) will be reduced to half because fewer light rays contribute to image formation
The image will turn upside down
questions.answer: Yes, a complete image of the entire object will still be formed, but its brightness (intensity) will be reduced to half because fewer light rays contribute to image formation
questions.explanation: Every uncovered portion of the lens refracts rays from every point of the object to form the full geometric image; covering half the aperture simply halves the transmitted light flux, dimming image brightness.

questions.question: A luminous object O and a screen S are placed 100 cm apart. A converging lens placed between them forms an image on the screen that is 4 times enlarged. What is the focal length (f) of the lens, and what is the object distance (u)?
Where should an object be placed in front of a convex lens to obtain a real image of the EXACT SAME SIZE as the object?
questions.explanation: When an object is placed at 2F1, the image forms at 2F2 on the other side, real, inverted, and of identical size (m = -1).

questions.question: Where must an object be placed to use a convex lens as a simple magnifying glass?
options: Between the optical centre (O) and the principal focus (F1)
questions.answer: Between the optical centre (O) and the principal focus (F1)
questions.explanation: When an object is placed between O and F1, the lens produces an upright, magnified virtual image on the same side.

questions.question: If the lower half of a convex lens is covered with opaque black paper, what will happen to the image of an object formed on a screen?
options: Only the upper half of the image is visible
The full image is formed, but its brightness (intensity) is reduced
The image is magnified twice as much
questions.answer: The full image is formed, but its brightness (intensity) is reduced
questions.explanation: Rays from every point of the object still pass through the uncovered half to form a complete image, but with half the light intensity.

questions.question: Where is the image formed when an object is placed between F1 and 2F1 in front of a convex lens?
questions.explanation: Placing an object between F1 and 2F1 produces a real, inverted, and magnified image beyond 2F2 (as in a movie projector).

questions.question: What type of image is produced by a convex lens when an object is at infinity?
options: Virtual and erect at the optical centre
Real, inverted, and highly diminished (point-sized) at focus F2
questions.answer: Real, inverted, and highly diminished (point-sized) at focus F2
questions.explanation: Parallel rays from infinity converge to the principal focus F2, forming a real, point-sized inverted image.

questions.question: Which of the following optical instruments uses a convex lens to cast an enlarged real image onto a photographic film or digital sensor?
questions.explanation: A camera utilizes a convex lens system to project real, inverted, and focused images onto a sensor or film.

title: Image Formation by Concave Lenses & Cartesian Sign Convention for Lenses
tagline: Always virtual, erect, and diminished images; New Cartesian sign rules for lenses.
theoryHtml:
1. Image Formation by a Concave Lens

A concave lens diverges all incident light rays outward. For any real object positioned at any finite distance in front of a concave lens:

  • Location: The image is always formed on the same side as the object, between the optical centre ($O$) and the focus ($F_1$).
  • Nature: The image is always virtual and erect.
  • Size: The image is always diminished (smaller than the object, $m < 1$).

2. New Cartesian Sign Convention for Lenses

Taking the optical centre ($O$) as the coordinate origin $(0,0)$:

  • Object Distance ($u$): Object is always placed to the left of the lens $\rightarrow u$ is always negative ($-$).
  • Focal Length of Convex Lens ($f$): The principal focus lies to the right ($+x$) $\rightarrow f$ is always positive ($+$).
  • Focal Length of Concave Lens ($f$): The principal focus lies to the left ($-x$) $\rightarrow f$ is always negative ($-$).
  • Real Image Distance ($v$): Formed on the opposite side (right, $+x$) $\rightarrow v$ is positive ($+$).
  • Virtual Image Distance ($v$): Formed on the same side as object (left, $-x$) $\rightarrow v$ is negative ($-$).
pointsToRemember: A concave lens ALWAYS forms virtual, erect, and diminished images on the same side as the object.
Focal length rules for lenses: Convex lens $f > 0$ (positive); Concave lens $f < 0$ (negative).
Real images in lenses have positive $v$; virtual images have negative $v$.
keyNotes: Note the crucial sign contrast with mirrors: for a lens, a real image formed on the opposite side has a POSITIVE image distance ($v > 0$).

questions.question: A concave lens ALWAYS produces an image that is:
options: Virtual, erect, and diminished, irrespective of object position
questions.answer: Virtual, erect, and diminished, irrespective of object position
questions.explanation: A diverging concave lens always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image located between the optical centre O and focus F₁.

questions.question: Under the New Cartesian Sign Convention, the focal length of a convex lens is always __________ and that of a concave lens is always __________.
questions.explanation: A convex lens has a positive focal length (+f), while a concave lens has a negative focal length (-f).

questions.question: A converging lens is submerged in a transparent liquid whose refractive index is EXACTLY EQUAL to the refractive index of the lens glass (n_liquid = n_lens). How will incident light rays behave inside the liquid?
options: They pass straight through without any refraction/deviation, and the lens becomes completely invisible in the liquid (focal length becomes infinite, Power = 0)
The lens acts as a mirror
questions.answer: They pass straight through without any refraction/deviation, and the lens becomes completely invisible in the liquid (focal length becomes infinite, Power = 0)
questions.explanation: When optical indices match, there is no change in light speed across the lens boundary (no refraction). The lens behaves like a continuous uniform medium (f = ∞, P = 0).

questions.question: What is the nature and size of the image formed by a concave lens for any finite object distance?
questions.explanation: A concave lens diverges rays, so backward ray projections always intersect between O and F1 to form a virtual, erect, diminished image.

questions.question: According to the New Cartesian Sign Convention, what is the sign of the focal length of a CONCAVE lens?
questions.explanation: The principal focus of a concave lens lies on the incident (left) side, so its focal length f is always negative.

questions.question: According to the New Cartesian Sign Convention, what is the sign of the focal length of a CONVEX lens?
questions.explanation: The primary focus of a convex lens where parallel rays converge lies to the right (+x direction), so f is positive.

questions.question: In a lens problem, if the calculated image distance is v = +24 cm, what does the positive sign indicate?
options: The image is virtual and on the left side
The image is real and formed on the opposite side (right side) of the lens
questions.answer: The image is real and formed on the opposite side (right side) of the lens
questions.explanation: In lenses, real rays pass through to the opposite (+x) side, giving a positive image distance (v > 0) for real images.

questions.question: Which of the following vision defects is corrected using a suitable CONCAVE (diverging) spectacle lens?
questions.explanation: A concave lens diverges incoming rays slightly before entering the eye, pushing the focused image back onto the myopic retina.

questions.question: Where is the image formed when an object is placed at infinity in front of a concave lens?
options: At the focus F1, point-sized and virtual
At infinity on the opposite side
questions.answer: At the focus F1, point-sized and virtual
questions.explanation: Parallel rays diverge upon entering the concave lens; their extensions meet at focus F1 as an upright, virtual, point-sized image.

questions.question: Can a concave lens ever produce an image larger than the object for a real object?
options: No, a concave lens always produces diminished images (|m| < 1)
questions.answer: No, a concave lens always produces diminished images (|m| < 1)
questions.explanation: A concave lens in air always produces a virtual, erect image that is strictly smaller than the object (0 < m < 1).

title: The Lens Formula & Linear Magnification
tagline: Mastery of 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, and magnification m = h'/h = +v/u.
theoryHtml:
1. The Lens Formula

The mathematical equation relating the object distance ($u$), image distance ($v$), and focal length ($f$) of a spherical lens is known as the Lens Formula:

$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$

Notice the crucial minus sign before $\frac{1}{u}$, which distinguishes the lens formula from the mirror formula ($\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$).

2. Linear Magnification ($m$) for Lenses

The magnification produced by a spherical lens is the ratio of the image height ($h'$) to the object height ($h$):

$$m = \frac{h'}{h} = +\frac{v}{u}$$

Notice that for lenses, $m = +\frac{v}{u}$ (has a positive sign), whereas for mirrors $m = -\frac{v}{u}$.

3. Interpreting Magnification for Lenses

  • Negative Magnification ($m < 0$): Image is real and inverted. (Because $v > 0$ and $u < 0$, $v/u$ is negative).
  • Positive Magnification ($m > 0$): Image is virtual and erect. (Because both $v < 0$ and $u < 0$, $v/u$ is positive).
  • $|m| > 1$: Image is magnified.
  • $|m| < 1$: Image is diminished.
  • $|m| = 1$: Image is same size as object.
pointsToRemember: The Lens Formula: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$.
Lens Magnification: $m = \frac{h'}{h} = +\frac{v}{u}$.
Negative $m$ signifies a real, inverted image; positive $m$ signifies a virtual, erect image.
keyNotes: Do not confuse mirror and lens formulas: Mirrors have $+1/u$ in formula and $-v/u$ in magnification; Lenses have $-1/u$ in formula and $+v/u$ in magnification.

questions.question: What is the correct Lens Formula relating object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f)?
questions.explanation: The thin lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.

questions.question: What is the formula for linear magnification (m) produced by a spherical lens?
questions.explanation: For spherical lenses, linear magnification m = h'/h = +v/u.

questions.question: An object 5.0 cm tall is placed at a distance of 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of radius of curvature R = 30 cm. What is the position (v), height (h'), and nature of the image?
options: v = -60 cm; h' = -15 cm; Real and inverted
v = +8.57 cm (behind mirror); h' = +2.14 cm; Virtual and erect
v = +15 cm; h' = +5.0 cm; Virtual and erect
v = -8.57 cm; h' = -2.14 cm; Real and inverted
questions.answer: v = +8.57 cm (behind mirror); h' = +2.14 cm; Virtual and erect

questions.question: Which of the following equations correctly represents the Lens Formula?
questions.explanation: The lens formula relates image distance v, object distance u, and focal length f through 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.

questions.question: What is the linear magnification formula for a spherical lens in terms of image distance (v) and object distance (u)?
questions.explanation: For spherical lenses, magnification is given by m = h'/h = +v/u.

questions.question: If a convex lens produces a real and inverted image of twice the height of the object, what is the magnification m?
questions.explanation: Because the image is real and inverted, m is negative; with height doubled, m = -2.

questions.question: A concave lens produces an image of height 2 cm from an object of height 6 cm. What is the magnification?
questions.explanation: A concave lens always produces an erect (positive) virtual image: m = h'/h = +2/6 = +1/3.

questions.question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. What is the image distance v?
What is the magnification in the question above (u = -30 cm, v = +60 cm)?
questions.explanation: For a lens, m = +v/u = (+60) / (-30) = -2 (real, inverted, magnified twice).

questions.question: If a lens produces a magnification of m = +1.5, what kind of lens is it and what is the nature of the image?
options: Convex lens acting as a magnifying glass, virtual and erect image
questions.answer: Convex lens acting as a magnifying glass, virtual and erect image
questions.explanation: Only a convex lens can produce a magnified (m > 1) virtual and erect (positive m) image when the object is within its focal length.

title: Power of a Lens ($P = 1/f$), The Dioptre & Thin Lens Combinations
tagline: Degree of convergence/divergence, SI unit Dioptre (D), and additive power in combination lenses.
theoryHtml:
1. Definition of Power of a Lens ($P$)

The power of a lens is a measure of its ability to converge or diverge incident light rays. A lens with a shorter focal length bends light rays through larger angles, focusing them closer to the optical centre, and therefore possesses greater optical power.

Mathematically, the power of a lens ($P$) is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length expressed in metres:

$$P = \frac{1}{f\text{ (in metres)}} = \frac{100}{f\text{ (in centimetres)}}$$

2. The SI Unit of Power: The Dioptre ($D$)

The SI unit of power of a lens is the dioptre, denoted by the symbol $\mathbf{D}$ ($1\text{ D} = 1\text{ m}^{-1}$):

"1 dioptre is the power of a lens whose focal length is exactly 1 metre."

3. Signs of Lens Power

  • Convex Lens: Focal length is positive ($f > 0$) $\implies$ Power is positive ($P > 0$). (e.g., $+2.0\text{ D}$).
  • Concave Lens: Focal length is negative ($f < 0$) $\implies$ Power is negative ($P < 0$). (e.g., $-1.5\text{ D}$).

4. Power of a Combination of Thin Lenses

When multiple thin lenses of powers $P_1, P_2, P_3, \dots$ are placed in direct contact, the net equivalent power ($P$) of the combination is simply the algebraic sum of the individual powers:

$$P = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 + \dots$$

This additive property is routinely used by opticians and camera lens designers to minimize optical aberrations.
pointsToRemember: Power of a lens is the reciprocal of focal length in metres: $P = 1/f\text{ (m)}$.
The SI unit of power is the Dioptre ($\text{D}$), where $1\text{ D} = 1\text{ m}^{-1}$.
Convex lenses have positive power ($P > 0$); concave lenses have negative power ($P < 0$).
Combined power in contact: $P = P_1 + P_2 + \dots$.
keyNotes: Always convert focal length into metres before calculating power: a focal length of $+20\text{ cm} = +0.2\text{ m}$ gives $P = 1/0.2 = +5\text{ D}$.

questions.question: The degree of convergence or divergence of light rays achieved by a lens is defined as its power (P). What is the formula for power P in terms of focal length f?
options: P = 1 / f (where f is in metres)
P = 100 / f (where f is in metres)
questions.answer: P = 1 / f (where f is in metres)
questions.explanation: Optical power is the reciprocal of focal length expressed in metres: P = 1 / f (in metres).

questions.question: What is the SI unit of power of a lens?
questions.explanation: The SI unit of lens power is dioptre (D), where 1 D = 1 m⁻¹.

questions.question: Define 1 dioptre (1 D) of power of a lens:
options: Power of a lens of focal length 1 cm
Power of a lens whose focal length is exactly 1 metre (1 D = 1 m⁻¹)
Power of a lens that absorbs all light
Power of a plane glass slab
questions.answer: Power of a lens whose focal length is exactly 1 metre (1 D = 1 m⁻¹)
questions.explanation: One dioptre is the optical power of a lens having a focal length of 1 metre.

questions.question: An optician prescribes a corrective lens of power P = +2.0 D. What is the nature and focal length of this lens?
options: Concave lens with focal length -0.50 m
Convex lens with focal length +0.50 m (+50 cm)
Convex lens with focal length +2.0 m
Plane lens with zero focal length
questions.answer: Convex lens with focal length +0.50 m (+50 cm)
questions.explanation: f = 1 / P = 1 / (+2.0 D) = +0.50 m = +50 cm. Positive power denotes a converging convex lens.

questions.question: What is the power of a concave lens having a focal length of 2 metres?
questions.explanation: For a concave lens, f = -2 m. Power P = 1 / f = 1 / (-2 m) = -0.5 D.

questions.question: What is the power of a convex lens having a focal length of 50 cm?
What is the focal length and nature of a lens having a power of -2.5 D?
questions.explanation: f = 1/P = 1/(-2.5) = -0.4 m = -40 cm. The negative sign signifies a concave (diverging) lens.

questions.question: Two thin lenses of powers +3.5 D and -1.5 D are placed in direct contact. What is the net power of the combination?
What is the equivalent focal length of the combined lens system in the question above (P = +2.0 D)?
questions.explanation: f = 1/P = 1/(+2.0 D) = +0.5 m = +50 cm (converging behaviour).

questions.question: Why do optometrists prescribe lens combinations in compound optical systems like microscopes?
options: To increase magnification and correct chromatic and spherical aberrations
To filter out all incoming red light
questions.answer: To increase magnification and correct chromatic and spherical aberrations
questions.explanation: Combining lenses of opposite sign allows designers to achieve sharp focus while eliminating chromatic and spherical distortions.

title: Comprehensive Optics Problem Solving: Mirrors, Lenses & Systems
tagline: Mastery problem-solving covering mirror formula, lens formula, magnification, and power calculations.
theoryHtml:
1. Summary of Master Equations in Optics

QuantitySpherical MirrorSpherical Lens
Fundamental Formula$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$
Focal Length ($f$)$f = \frac{R}{2}$$f = \frac{1}{P\text{ (m)}}$
Linear Magnification ($m$)$m = \frac{h'}{h} = -\frac{v}{u}$$m = \frac{h'}{h} = +\frac{v}{u}$
Convex Element Sign$f > 0$$f > 0$, $P > 0$
Concave Element Sign$f < 0$$f < 0$, $P < 0$
Object Distance ($u$)Always negative ($-$)Always negative ($-$)

2. Systematic Checklist for Solving Board Exam Numericals

  1. Identify whether the optical element is a Mirror or a Lens.
  2. Identify whether it is Convex or Concave.
  3. Write down all given values ($u, v, f, h, P$) with their explicit Cartesian signs.
  4. Select the appropriate equation and solve algebraically before inserting numbers.
  5. Verify the physical realism: check if magnification signs match the real/virtual nature of the image!
pointsToRemember: Mirrors: $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ and $m = -\frac{v}{u}$.
Lenses: $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ and $m = +\frac{v}{u}$.
Power: $P = 1/f\text{ (m)}$; combined lenses: $P = P_1 + P_2$.
keyNotes: Always double-check units: convert cm to m when calculating Power in Dioptres, and convert m to cm when comparing with object/image distances.

questions.question: An object 7.0 cm high is placed at a distance of 27 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 18 cm. At what distance should a screen be placed to obtain a sharp image, and what is the height and nature of the image?
options: v = -54 cm (54 cm in front of mirror); h' = -14.0 cm; Real and inverted
v = +54 cm; h' = +14.0 cm; Virtual and erect
v = -18 cm; h' = -7.0 cm; Real and inverted
v = -36 cm; h' = -10.5 cm; Real and inverted
questions.answer: v = -54 cm (54 cm in front of mirror); h' = -14.0 cm; Real and inverted
questions.explanation: Concave mirror: f = -18 cm, u = -27 cm. 1/v = 1/(-18) - 1/(-27) = -1/18 + 1/27 = -1/54 ⇒ v = -54 cm. Screen at 54 cm in front. m = -v/u = -(-54)/(-27) = -2. h' = m × h = -2 × 7.0 cm = -14.0 cm (Real, inverted, 2x enlarged).

questions.question: An illuminated object 2.0 cm high is placed perpendicular to the principal axis of a converging convex lens of focal length 10 cm at an object distance of 15 cm. What is the image position (v), magnification (m), and image height (h')?
options: v = +30 cm (on other side); m = -2; h' = -4.0 cm (Real, inverted, enlarged)
questions.answer: v = +30 cm (on other side); m = -2; h' = -4.0 cm (Real, inverted, enlarged)

questions.question: A composite lens system consists of three thin lenses in contact: Lens 1 (convex, f₁ = +20 cm), Lens 2 (concave, f₂ = -50 cm), and Lens 3 (convex, f₃ = +25 cm). What is the net power (P) and equivalent focal length (F) of the combination?
Light travels from medium A into medium B. The angle of incidence is 45° and the angle of refraction is 30°. What is the refractive index of medium B with respect to medium A (nBA)?
Why does the sun appear slightly oval/flattened at sunrise and sunset?
options: Atmospheric refraction bends light rays from the lower edge of the solar disc more strongly than rays from the upper edge due to vertical density gradients in atmospheric air
Clouds physically block the top and bottom
questions.answer: Atmospheric refraction bends light rays from the lower edge of the solar disc more strongly than rays from the upper edge due to vertical density gradients in atmospheric air
questions.explanation: The atmospheric density gradient causes differential upward refraction: rays from the lower limb travel through denser air and bend more than rays from the upper limb, causing apparent vertical compression.

questions.question: In an optical bench experiment, a student obtains a sharp image of a candle flame on a screen using a concave mirror. If the lower half of the mirror is completely covered with black cardboard, what changes will occur on the screen?
options: The upper half of the flame image disappears
The full image of the flame remains visible on the screen, but its illumination brightness is halved
questions.answer: The full image of the flame remains visible on the screen, but its illumination brightness is halved
questions.explanation: Every point of the reflecting surface reflects rays originating from all points of the object; covering the lower half reduces the total light energy collected by 50% without altering image geometry.

questions.question: What is the physical condition under which a ray of light passing from an optically denser medium into an optically rarer medium undergoes Total Internal Reflection?
options: Angle of incidence (i) in the denser medium exceeds the critical angle (C) for that pair of media (sin C = 1 / n)
Both media have equal refractive index
Light must be monochromatic red only
questions.answer: Angle of incidence (i) in the denser medium exceeds the critical angle (C) for that pair of media (sin C = 1 / n)
questions.explanation: When light travels from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle of incidence greater than the critical angle (i > C), it cannot refract (r > 90°) and is 100% reflected back into the denser medium.

questions.question: A ray of light traveling in water (nw = 4/3) is incident on a glass plate (ng = 3/2). What is the refractive index of glass with respect to water (ngw)?
A virtual image formed by a concave mirror is ALWAYS __________ the object, while a virtual image formed by a convex mirror is ALWAYS __________ the object.
questions.explanation: A concave mirror's virtual image (object between P and F) is always magnified (m > 1). A convex mirror's virtual image is always diminished (0 < m < 1).

questions.question: A concave lens has focal length of 15 cm. At what distance should the object from the lens be placed so that it forms an image at 10 cm from the lens?
questions.explanation: For a concave lens, f = -15 cm, and image is virtual so v = -10 cm. 1/f = 1/v - 1/u => 1/u = 1/v - 1/f = 1/(-10) - 1/(-15) = -1/10 + 1/15 = -1/30 => u = -30 cm.
